question: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

Over the last few days, there have been continuous attacks on the city of Suqaylabiyah – a city with a predominantly Orthodox population. Syria has always been a state with a rich multicultural identity, in which Muslims (Sunni and Shia), Kurds, Druze, Christians of various denominations, Armenians and other minorities have coexisted. Unfortunately, the interim government does not seem to share this conviction in practice, as in recent months we have seen a significant increase in attacks against religious and ethnic minorities, often with the support – if not the participation – of government-aligned forces. As Orthodox Christians prepare to celebrate Easter, and bearing in mind that the European Union is one of Syria’s principal donors, will the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy say: 1.
What will she do to protect Syria’s multicultural character and its religious and ethnic minorities, in particular Orthodox Christians, who face constant persecution?
Is she willing to impose new sanctions if the interim government continues to allow and support the attacks against them?
Is she committed to ensuring that any financial or other support for the regime in Syria is conditional on the protection of all religious and ethnic minorities?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.6.2026) Since the historic shift in the country in December 2024, the EU has actively supported Syria through every stage of their challenging transition. The EU’s strategy is founded on the belief that lasting peace and stability can only be achieved through an inclusive transition that meets the aspirations of Syrians from all ethnic and religious backgrounds without discrimination. The EU also calls upon all involved parties to safeguard Syria’s diverse cultural heritage and religious sites. In response to the documented incidents, the EU persists in calling for thorough investigations and ensuring that all those responsible for violence in Syria are held to account. Within its discussions with Syria’s transitional authorities, the EU reiterates that this is instrumental for pursuing national reconciliation and an inclusive transition. During their visit to Syria, the Presidents of the European Council and the Commission unveiled a new EU-Syria Political Partnership1, designed to support the political transition, national reconciliation and reconstruction. On 11 May 2026, the EU held its first High-Level Political Dialogue with Syria in Brussels, where inter alia the need to ensure a genuinely inclusive process for sustainable reconciliation and restoring Syria’s rich social fabric was underscored. The EU remains vigilant about the respect for human rights of all Syrians and will continue to support comprehensive accountability efforts for all perpetrators regardless of their affiliation. In May2 and June3 2025, the EU introduced new listings against human rights violators and will continue monitoring the situation on the ground and the follow up of the commitments of the transitional authorities. Protecting the rights of most vulnerable ethnic and religious communities is essential to ensuring social cohesion, preventing further sectarian divisions, and laying the foundations for a sustainable and inclusive peace, as reiterated in the Council conclusions of 18 December 20254.
